questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.

Intensive Care Med
https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-019-05529-w
ORIGINAL
Nasal high-flow preoxygenation
for endotracheal intubation in the critically ill
patient: a randomized clinical trial
Christophe Guitton1*, Stephan Ehrmann2, Christelle Volteau3, Gwenhael Colin4, Adel Maamar5,
Vanessa Jean-Michel6, Pierre-Joachim Mahe7, Mickael Landais1, Noelle Brule8, Cedric Bretonnière8,
Olivier Zambon8 and Mickael Vourc'h8
© 2019 Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature
Abstract
Purpose: Preoxygenation with high-flow therapy by nasal cannulae (HFNC) is now widespread in the intensive care
unit (ICU). However, no large randomized study has assessed its relevance in non-severely hypoxemic patients. In a
randomized controlled trial (PROTRACH study), we aimed to evaluate preoxygenation with HFNC vs. standard bag-
valve mask oxygenation (SMO) in non-severely hypoxemic patients during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in the ICU.
Methods: Randomized controlled trial including non-severely hypoxemic patients requiring intubation in the ICU.
Patients received preoxygenation by HFNC or SMO during RSI. HFNC was maintained throughout the intubation
procedure whereas SMO was removed to perform laryngoscopy. The primary outcome was the lowest pulse oximetry
(SpO2) throughout the intubation procedure. Secondary outcomes included drop in SpO2, adverse events related to
intubation, and outcome in the ICU.
Results: A total of 192 patients were randomized. In the intent-to-treat analysis, 184 patients (HFNC n = 95; SMO
n = 89), the median [IQR] lowest SpO2 was 100% [97; 100] for HFNC and 99% [95; 100] for the SMO group (P = 0.30).
Mild desaturation below 95% was more frequent with SMO (23%) than with HFNC (12%) (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.26-0.99,
P = 0.045). There were fewer adverse events in the HFNC group (6%) than in the SMO group (19%) (RR 0.31, 95% CI
0.13-0.76, P = 0.007), including fewer severe adverse events, respectively 6 (6%) and 14 (16%) with HFNC and SMO (RR
0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.95, P = 0.03).
Conclusions: Compared with SMO, preoxygenation with HFNC in the ICU did not improve the lowest SpO2 during
intubation in the non-severely hypoxemic patients but led to a reduction in intubation-related adverse events.
Trial registration: Clinical trial Submission: 7 March 2016. Registry name: Benefits of high-flow nasal cannulae oxy-
gen for preoxygenation during intubation in non-severely hypoxemic patients: the PROTRACH study. Clinicaltrials.gov

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

1|Introduction
2|Endotracheal intubation is a procedure that is performed
3|daily in the intensive care units (ICU). Nevertheless, it
4|remains a life-threatening event and causes more than
5|25% of severe complications such as oxygen desaturation,
6|hemodynamic instability, and death [1-3], driving inten-
7|sive research efforts in the field [4-6].
8|Preoxygenation is a key component of intubation in
9|order to stock up oxygen in functional residual capacity
10|(FRC) volume, representing the main oxygen reservoir
11|during apnea [7]. After the induction of general anes-
12|thesia, it extends the duration of apnea until hypoxemia
13|occurs, i.e., oxygen desaturation below a critical pulse
14|oximetry (SpO2) value [8]. In critically ill patients, several
15|pathological conditions compromise optimal preoxygen-
16|ation such as high peripheral oxygen uptake, hemody-
17|namic instability, or altered consciousness. In this setting,
18|preoxygenation with the standard bag-valve mask oxy-
19|genation (SMO) followed by rapid sequence intubation
20|(RSI) is proposed [9] to reduce the risk of desaturation
21|and aspiration. RSI includes immediate intubation after
22|hypnotic administration without manual face mask venti-
23|lation to minimize the time from induction to intubation.
24|SMO is removed during laryngoscopy-meaning that
25|oxygenation of the patient is interrupted. Alternatives
26|such as high-flow therapy by nasal cannulae (HFNC)
27|could prove beneficial. Indeed, considering the encour-
28|aging results in patients presenting acute hypoxemic
29|respiratory failure [10], HFNC has been proposed as a
30|preoxygenation device for intubation in the ICU. This
31|device can deliver up to 60 L/min with an inspired frac-
32|tion of oxygen of up to 100% [11], generate a moderate
33|positive supraglottic end-expiratory pressure, and reduce
34|the patient effort [12]. Contrary to SMO, HFNC makes it
35|possible to hold nasal prongs in place after induction of
36|general anesthesia and during laryngoscopy, to perform
37|apneic oxygenation throughout the intubation proce-
38|dure [13]. Furthermore, tolerance of HFNC has repeat-
39|edly been shown to be excellent whereas SMO can cause
40|discomfort and claustrophobia since the mask is tightly
41|applied to the patient [14]. HFNC is a widespread device
42|in the ICU but there is no large randomized study that
43|has evaluated its benefits as a preoxygenation device
44|for intubation in non-severely hypoxemic patients.
45|We recently reported that this device failed to prevent
46|desaturation during intubation in severely hypoxemic
47|patients [3]. In non-severely hypoxemic patients, a recent
48|before-after study suggested that HFNC could improve
49|preoxygenation and reduce severe hypoxemia during
50|intubation [15].
51|The main objective was to determine the efficacy of
52|HFNC for preoxygenation compared with SMO as meas-
53|ured by the lowest level of pulse oximetry during RSI
54|recorded through SpO2. Secondary objectives were to
55|compare intubation procedures, related side effects, and
56|patient outcome in the two groups.
57|Methods
58|Study design, setting, and ethical considerations
59|The PROTRACH study was a multicenter, randomized,
60|controlled, open-label clinical trial. The main objective
61|was to determine the efficacy of HFNC to prevent oxy-
62|gen desaturation during intubation in the ICU compared
63|with standard of care. Patients were enrolled from April
64|2016 to June 2017 in seven French ICUs (four medical,
65|two medical-surgical, and one surgical) and followed for
66|28 days. An independent safety committee oversaw the
67|trial.
68|Three methods of consent were available; patients
69|were included after written informed consent whenever
70|possible. Most patients were included after the written
71|informed consent of their next-of-kin or following an
72|emergency inclusion procedure. The appropriate ethics
73|committee approved this study protocol in September
74|2015 (15/13-975).
75|Participants
76|Eligible patients were adults (18 years or older), requir-
77|ing intubation in the ICU, without severe hypoxemia
78|defined as a ratio of arterial partial pressure in oxygen to
79|fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) below 200 within
80|4 h before inclusion. To determine the PaO2/FiO2 ratio
81|on inclusion, the FiO2 specified by the manufacturer for
82|Venturi mask or corresponding to the oxygen flow for
83|standard nasal prongs [16] was considered.
84|Exclusion criteria were intubation without rapid
85|sequence induction (i.e., in case of cardiac arrest),
86|fiberoptic intubation, asphyxia requiring immediate
87|Keywords: Preoxygenation, High-flow oxygen therapy by nasal cannulae, Intubation, Apneic oxygenation, Intensive
88|care unit
89|Take-home message
90|This is the first randomized multicenter study comparing the use of
91|HFNC with SMO for the preoxygenation of non-severely hypoxemic
92|patients in the ICU. In this setting, compared to SMO, preoxygena-
93|tion with HFNC did not improve the lowest SpO2 during intubation
94|but led to a reduction in intubation-related adverse events.

1|intubation, any nasopharyngeal anatomical obstacle,
2|grade 4 glottis exposure on the Cormack-Lehane scale
3|documented in the medical history, adults subject to legal
4|protection, pregnancy, lack of consent, patients who had
5|already undergone intubation in the ICU (i.e., extubation
6|failure) or who were already participating in an interven-
7|tional study on preoxygenation.
8|Randomization
9|Randomization used fixed blocks of six patients (ratio
10|1:1) and was stratified by center. The study statistician
11|generated the allocation list. Patients were allocated to
12|one of the two preoxygenation strategies using a secure
13|computer-generated online remote system controlled
14|by the independent research promotion unit at the Uni-
15|versity Hospital of Nantes which had no role in patient
16|recruitment.
17|Intervention: preoxygenation and intubation procedure
18|The study design is described in Supplement 1. Preoxy-
19|genation and intubation were performed according to
20|international recommendations in all centers [9]. The
21|intubation team was composed of one junior and one
22|senior.
23|1. Preoxygenation was started according to the rand-
24|omization group for a 4-min period [17] in a head-up
25|position. In the intervention group, preoxygenation
26|was performed with HFNC (AIRVO 2TM; Fisher &
27|Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, NZ), nasal prongs set at
28|60 L/min flow of heated and humidified pure oxygen
29|(100% fraction of inspired oxygen, 37 °C). Large or
30|medium nasal cannulae were chosen according to the
31|patient's nostril size to limit air contamination. In the
32|control group, preoxygenation was performed with
33|SMO set at 15 L/min oxygen flow with a disposable
34|self-inflating resuscitator with a reservoir bag manu-
35|ally held in place ensuring air tightness.
36|2. At the end of preoxygenation, RSI including imme-
37|diate intubation after administration of the hypnotic
38|drugs was performed in all patients. Drugs and the
39|use of a neuromuscular blocking agent were left to
40|the discretion of the physician.
41|3. During laryngoscopy and intubation, HFNC was
42|maintained in place throughout the procedure in an
43|attempt to achieve apneic oxygenation. In the control
44|group, SMO was removed in order to perform laryn-
45|goscopy.
46|4. In case of difficult intubation, the stylet was the first
47|alternative device which was proposed [18] if exter-
48|nal laryngeal manipulation did not improve glottis
49|vision.
50|5. At the end of intubation, the correct position of the
51|tracheal tube was confirmed by using capnography
52|[19].
53|Endpoints
54|The primary endpoint was the median lowest SpO2 dur-
55|ing intubation, from the beginning of the laryngoscopy
56|until the patient was connected to the mechanical ven-
57|tilator. To ensure exhaustive data collection, a research
58|nurse and an external observer concurrently collected
59|SpO2 fluctuations during the intubation.
60|Secondary endpoints were SpO2 from the beginning
61|of preoxygenation to the end of intubation focusing on
62|desaturation (below 95%, 90%, 80%); the rate of difficult
63|intubation [20] and the intubation difficulty scale (IDS)
64|score [21]; the need to proceed to face mask ventilation
65|to correct desaturation; adverse events a priori classified
66|as severe (death, cardiac arrest, SpO2 < 80%, severe hypo-
67|tension defined by systolic blood pressure < 80 mmHg or
68|vasopressor initiation or 30% dose increment) or moder-
69|ate (ventricular or supraventricular arrhythmia requir-
70|ing intervention, esophageal intubation, vomiting with
71|aspiration of gastric content, dental injury); organ failure
72|during the first 5 days (SOFA score); time on the ventila-
73|tor; length of stay in ICU; occurrence of ventilator-asso-
74|ciated pneumonia and mortality rate on day 28 (full study
75|protocol appears in Supplement 2).
76|Sample size
77|On the basis of previous studies we hypothesized that
78|HFNC would improve the mean lowest SpO2 value by
79|5% (from 88% in the control group to 93% in the HFNC
80|group) with a standard deviation of SpO2 of 12% [15,
81|22]. With 80% power, a 5% type I error (two-sided tests),
82|and 5% attrition rate, the required sample size was 192
83|patients.
84|Statistical analysis
85|Baseline characteristics were described as count and per-
86|centage for categorical variables and mean and standard
87|deviation or median and interquartiles for quantitative
88|variables when assumption of normality was not met. An
89|intent-to-treat statistical analysis was conducted. Com-
90|parisons of primary and secondary outcomes were per-
91|formed using the Mantel-Haenszel Chi-square tests (or
92|two-tailed Fisher exact tests when appropriate) for quali-
93|tative data and the Van Elteren tests for quantitative data
94|to account for stratification factor (center). For qualitative
95|data, relative risk (with adjustment for center effects) and
96|95% confidence interval were estimated with the Mantel-
97|Haenszel method. Multivariable analysis of SpO2 < 90%,
98|SpO2 < 80%, and the occurrence of adverse events were
99|performed using logistic regression. The most clinically

1|relevant variables (skills of the first operator, difficult
2|intubation, MACOCHA score ≥ 3, and PaO2/FiO2 ratio
3|at baseline) or associated with the randomization group
4|(P values < 0.20) in univariate analysis (age and NYHA
5|class) were introduced simultaneously into the models.
6|Odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were
7|estimated. All tests were two-tailed. P values of less than
8|0.05 were considered significant. No data was missing
9|for the primary outcome. For secondary outcomes, miss-
10|ing data were clearly stated in the tables (see also Sup-
11|plement 3), and no method of imputation was used. SAS
12|software version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc.) was used.
13|Results
14|Patients
15|In the seven participating ICUs, 192 patients were rand-
16|omized in the study between April 2016 and June 2017.
17|Three patients withdrew their consent, two patients were
18|discovered to be under guardianship protection, and
19|three patients improved before the start of the study and
20|were therefore not intubated. We considered 184 patients
21|(95 in HFNC and 89 in SMO) in the intent-to-treat
22|(ITT) and 183 patients in the per-protocol (PP) analyses
23|(Fig. 1). Per-protocol analysis excluded the only patient
24|with protocol deviation in the HFNC group who did not
25|receive preoxygenation with HFNC because no device
26|was available. This patient did not present any complica-
27|tion during intubation.
28|At baseline, patients were mainly intubation for a
29|medical condition with a median [interquartile range,
30|IQR] simplified acute physiology score 2 (SAPS II) of
31|45 [35; 60] in HFNC and 41 [32; 57] in SMO; median
32|[IQR] PaO2/FiO2 was 318 mmHg [242; 396] in HFNC
33|and 375 mmHg [276; 446] in SMO. In the two groups,
34|intubation was mainly performed for neurologic reasons
35|in comatose patients: 68% in HFNC and 75% in SMO
36|(Table 1). In order to prevent hypotension, fluid loading
37|was performed before anesthesia induction in 41 (43%)
38|patients in HFNC vs. 37 (42%) in SMO. Airways, opera-
39|tors, and technical aspects of intubation are described
40|in Table 2. Mean (standard deviation, SD) MACOCHA
41|score to predict difficult intubation was 2.0 (1.6) in

answer_anchors.text: Carers or intervention personnel were aware of assigned intervention.
Carers or intervention personnel were blinded to assigned intervention.

questions.bias_construct: Whether carers and people delivering interventions were aware of participants' assigned intervention.
considerations: Assess the people delivering interventions, not merely outcome assessors.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when carers or intervention personnel knew assignment, including when participant side effects or toxicities revealed it. If randomized allocation was not concealed, awareness by carers and delivery personnel is likely.
evidence_needed: A direct report of blinding or awareness by carers and people delivering the intervention, plus the allocation process when it bears on their awareness.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when awareness of carers or delivery personnel cannot be determined.
questions.official_guidance: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.2
questions.wording: Were carers and people delivering the interventions aware of participants' assigned intervention during the trial?

answer_anchors.text: The trial context caused protocol-inconsistent deviations.
No protocol-inconsistent deviation arose because of the trial context.
Reported details and trial circumstances do not support a judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.

questions.bias_construct: Whether deviations inconsistent with protocol arose because of the trial context.
considerations: Side-effect-related compromised blinding counts only when resulting changes were protocol-inconsistent and context-caused.

Subsequent treatment, rescue treatment, or cross-over is not itself a deviation for the effect of assignment: establish both protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause before answering affirmatively.

Neutral contrast: protocol-permitted rescue after progression is ordinary subsequent care; prohibited rescue encouraged by trial staff is a candidate trial-context deviation. Change only the protocol-consistency and cause premises before changing the reasoning.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes only after establishing both that the change was inconsistent with the protocol and that the trial context caused it; identify both premises in the justification. Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.
invalid_shortcuts: unequal post-progression treatment without evidence that it was prohibited and trial-context-caused
a protocol deviation without its cause
discontinuation or crossover without protocol and cause evidence
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when reported details are insufficient and trial circumstances do not support a reasonable probable judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.3
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2: Were there deviations from the intended intervention that arose because of the trial context?

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
The identified deviations were not likely to affect the outcome.

questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
considerations: This question concerns the deviations already identified in 2.3, not any non-adherence in isolation.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were likely to affect the intervention effect estimate through this outcome; answer no or probably no when they were not likely to affect the outcome.
evidence_needed: A direct link between the identified context-caused deviation and this outcome or its effect estimate.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the effect of the identified deviations on the outcome cannot be determined.
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context will impact on the intervention effect estimate if they affect the outcome, but not otherwise.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4
questions.wording: If Y/PY to 2.3: Were these deviations likely to have affected the outcome?

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
The identified deviations were not balanced between intervention groups.

questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were balanced between groups; answer no or probably no when they were not balanced.
evidence_needed: Group-specific counts or descriptions of the identified deviations and their comparability between intervention groups.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when balance of the identified deviations cannot be determined.
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.5
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.4: Were these deviations from intended intervention balanced between groups?

answer_anchors.text: An ITT or appropriate modified ITT analysis estimated assignment effect.
A naive per-protocol, as-treated, or inappropriate post-randomization exclusion analysis was used.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

Excluding participants solely because their outcome data are missing can be an appropriate modified ITT analysis for D2; assess the missing outcomes in D3. An eligible participant with an observed outcome omitted from the assignment analysis, or analysed in the wrong randomized group, is a distinct D2 concern. Record whether exclusions occurred before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded, but timing alone does not establish availability or the exclusion reason. An observed value omitted from analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. An analyzed count below the randomized count alone does not establish inappropriate analysis; if the exclusion mechanism cannot support a reasonable probable judgment, retain no_information. When 2.6 is no, probably_no, or no_information, assess 2.7 conditionally: could the wrong-group analysis or exclusions substantially affect this Result if the assignment-analysis failure occurred? Keep uncertainty about the analysis mechanism explicit. Assess potential impact using the participants affected, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance; demonstrated actual bias or a sensitivity analysis is not required, and no precise percentage rule applies.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
questions.wording: Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?

answer_anchors.text: The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could substantially affect the result.
The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could not substantially affect the result.

questions.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
considerations: This is conditional on an inappropriate or uncertain analysis in 2.6.
Assess potential impact only after deciding whether 2.6 was appropriate; a small or balanced exclusion can have low impact without making an inappropriate analysis appropriate.

Use facts about this endpoint and the excluded participants. Exclusion before outcome ascertainment may also leave outcome data missing; exclusion after ascertainment may omit observed values from the analysis. Neither timing alone settles the possible effect on the estimate.
questions.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.
invalid_shortcuts: a group label without exclusion counts
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the potential magnitude of impact cannot be assessed.
questions.official_guidance: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.7
questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 2.6: Was there potential for a substantial impact (on the result) of the failure to analyse participants in the group to which they were randomized?

intubation, any nasopharyngeal anatomical obstacle,
grade 4 glottis exposure on the Cormack-Lehane scale
documented in the medical history, adults subject to legal
protection, pregnancy, lack of consent, patients who had
already undergone intubation in the ICU (i.e., extubation
failure) or who were already participating in an interven-
tional study on preoxygenation.
Randomization
Randomization used fixed blocks of six patients (ratio
1:1) and was stratified by center. The study statistician
generated the allocation list. Patients were allocated to
one of the two preoxygenation strategies using a secure
computer-generated online remote system controlled
by the independent research promotion unit at the Uni-
versity Hospital of Nantes which had no role in patient
recruitment.
Intervention: preoxygenation and intubation procedure
The study design is described in Supplement 1. Preoxy-
genation and intubation were performed according to
international recommendations in all centers [9]. The
intubation team was composed of one junior and one
senior.
1. Preoxygenation was started according to the rand-
omization group for a 4-min period [17] in a head-up
position. In the intervention group, preoxygenation
was performed with HFNC (AIRVO 2TM; Fisher &
Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, NZ), nasal prongs set at
60 L/min flow of heated and humidified pure oxygen
(100% fraction of inspired oxygen, 37 °C). Large or
medium nasal cannulae were chosen according to the
patient's nostril size to limit air contamination. In the
control group, preoxygenation was performed with
SMO set at 15 L/min oxygen flow with a disposable
self-inflating resuscitator with a reservoir bag manu-
ally held in place ensuring air tightness.
2. At the end of preoxygenation, RSI including imme-
diate intubation after administration of the hypnotic
drugs was performed in all patients. Drugs and the
use of a neuromuscular blocking agent were left to
the discretion of the physician.
3. During laryngoscopy and intubation, HFNC was
maintained in place throughout the procedure in an
attempt to achieve apneic oxygenation. In the control
group, SMO was removed in order to perform laryn-
goscopy.
4. In case of difficult intubation, the stylet was the first
alternative device which was proposed [18] if exter-
nal laryngeal manipulation did not improve glottis
vision.
5. At the end of intubation, the correct position of the
tracheal tube was confirmed by using capnography
[19].
Endpoints
The primary endpoint was the median lowest SpO2 dur-
ing intubation, from the beginning of the laryngoscopy
until the patient was connected to the mechanical ven-
tilator. To ensure exhaustive data collection, a research
nurse and an external observer concurrently collected
SpO2 fluctuations during the intubation.
Secondary endpoints were SpO2 from the beginning
of preoxygenation to the end of intubation focusing on
desaturation (below 95%, 90%, 80%); the rate of difficult
intubation [20] and the intubation difficulty scale (IDS)
score [21]; the need to proceed to face mask ventilation
to correct desaturation; adverse events a priori classified
as severe (death, cardiac arrest, SpO2 < 80%, severe hypo-
tension defined by systolic blood pressure < 80 mmHg or
vasopressor initiation or 30% dose increment) or moder-
ate (ventricular or supraventricular arrhythmia requir-
ing intervention, esophageal intubation, vomiting with
aspiration of gastric content, dental injury); organ failure
during the first 5 days (SOFA score); time on the ventila-
tor; length of stay in ICU; occurrence of ventilator-asso-
ciated pneumonia and mortality rate on day 28 (full study
protocol appears in Supplement 2).
Sample size
On the basis of previous studies we hypothesized that
HFNC would improve the mean lowest SpO2 value by
5% (from 88% in the control group to 93% in the HFNC
group) with a standard deviation of SpO2 of 12% [15,
22]. With 80% power, a 5% type I error (two-sided tests),
and 5% attrition rate, the required sample size was 192
patients.
Statistical analysis
Baseline characteristics were described as count and per-
centage for categorical variables and mean and standard
deviation or median and interquartiles for quantitative
variables when assumption of normality was not met. An
intent-to-treat statistical analysis was conducted. Com-
parisons of primary and secondary outcomes were per-
formed using the Mantel-Haenszel Chi-square tests (or
two-tailed Fisher exact tests when appropriate) for quali-
tative data and the Van Elteren tests for quantitative data
to account for stratification factor (center). For qualitative
data, relative risk (with adjustment for center effects) and
95% confidence interval were estimated with the Mantel-
Haenszel method. Multivariable analysis of SpO2 < 90%,
SpO2 < 80%, and the occurrence of adverse events were
performed using logistic regression. The most clinically

relevant variables (skills of the first operator, difficult
intubation, MACOCHA score ≥ 3, and PaO2/FiO2 ratio
at baseline) or associated with the randomization group
(P values < 0.20) in univariate analysis (age and NYHA
class) were introduced simultaneously into the models.
Odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were
estimated. All tests were two-tailed. P values of less than
0.05 were considered significant. No data was missing
for the primary outcome. For secondary outcomes, miss-
ing data were clearly stated in the tables (see also Sup-
plement 3), and no method of imputation was used. SAS
software version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc.) was used.
Results
Patients
In the seven participating ICUs, 192 patients were rand-
omized in the study between April 2016 and June 2017.
Three patients withdrew their consent, two patients were
discovered to be under guardianship protection, and
three patients improved before the start of the study and
were therefore not intubated. We considered 184 patients
(95 in HFNC and 89 in SMO) in the intent-to-treat
(ITT) and 183 patients in the per-protocol (PP) analyses
(Fig. 1). Per-protocol analysis excluded the only patient
with protocol deviation in the HFNC group who did not
receive preoxygenation with HFNC because no device
was available. This patient did not present any complica-
tion during intubation.
At baseline, patients were mainly intubation for a
medical condition with a median [interquartile range,
IQR] simplified acute physiology score 2 (SAPS II) of
45 [35; 60] in HFNC and 41 [32; 57] in SMO; median
[IQR] PaO2/FiO2 was 318 mmHg [242; 396] in HFNC
and 375 mmHg [276; 446] in SMO. In the two groups,
intubation was mainly performed for neurologic reasons
in comatose patients: 68% in HFNC and 75% in SMO
(Table 1). In order to prevent hypotension, fluid loading
was performed before anesthesia induction in 41 (43%)
patients in HFNC vs. 37 (42%) in SMO. Airways, opera-
tors, and technical aspects of intubation are described
in Table 2. Mean (standard deviation, SD) MACOCHA
score to predict difficult intubation was 2.0 (1.6) in
HFNC and 2.2 (2.0) in SMO [23]. There was no between-
group difference in doses or nature of hypnotics (see
Supplement 3). All intubations were performed with two
operators including a senior and the first operators were
mainly (84%) juniors. In the HFNC group, cannula sizes
were large for 45% and medium for 55%. No patient was
lost to follow-up (see Supplement 3).
Primary outcome: lowest SpO2 during the intubation
procedure
In the intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis (Table 3, Fig. 2),
there was no significant difference between the median
[IQR] lowest SpO2 during intubation in the HFNC group
compared with the SMO group, 100% [97; 100] versus
99% [95; 100] respectively, (P = 0.30). In the per-protocol
(PP) analysis (attrition rate 1%), the lack of difference per-
sisted (P = 0.26). Although only non-severely hypoxemic
patients were included, the lowest SpO2 during intuba-
tion ranged from 69% to 100% in HFNC and from 43% to
100% in SMO.

paired_examples.changed_premise: whether the same allocation-driven conduct was protocol-consistent
left_facts: The treating clinician reported that knowledge of experimental allocation prompted rescue treatment. The protocol permitted that rescue.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Hold the documented allocation-driven cause fixed while changing protocol consistency.
right_facts: The same treating clinician reported that knowledge of experimental allocation prompted the same rescue treatment. The protocol prohibited that rescue.

paired_examples.changed_premise: the documented reason for the same clinician's prohibited conduct
left_facts: The protocol prohibited rescue treatment. The treating clinician provided rescue because of the patient's symptoms, as the clinician would in ordinary care.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Hold protocol inconsistency, personnel and conduct fixed; distinguish ordinary care from an allocation-driven decision. Personnel identity alone supplies no cause.
right_facts: The protocol prohibited rescue treatment. The same treating clinician provided the same rescue because knowledge of experimental allocation changed the decision.

paired_examples.changed_premise: the documented reason for stopping the same assigned program
left_facts: The protocol required twelve exercise sessions. A participant stopped because the assigned exercises were physically difficult, as could occur in ordinary treatment.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Keep non-adherence fixed. Treatment burden and trial-specific engagement are different causes; insufficient cause information remains unresolved.
right_facts: The same protocol required twelve exercise sessions. A participant stopped the same program because additional research-only appointments prevented attendance.

paired_examples.changed_premise: the source-stated exclusion rule and outcome availability
left_facts: Of 100 eligible randomized participants, 90 were analyzed in assigned groups. The report states that only the ten with unmeasured endpoint outcomes were excluded; adherence did not restrict the analysis.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: The same analysis count can reflect missing-only availability or an adherence-conditioned rule. Source-stated observed outcomes omitted from analysis are affirmative evidence, not merely an uncertain denominator.
right_facts: Of the same 100 eligible randomized participants, 90 were analyzed in assigned groups. The report states that only treatment completers were analyzed even though endpoint outcomes were measured for all 100.

paired_examples.changed_premise: whether the source establishes an exclusion rule
left_facts: Of 100 eligible randomized participants, 90 completed treatment and 90 were analyzed. Some noncompleters were contactable, but their endpoint measurement and the analysis restriction are not reported.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Compatible counts do not identify a rule; contact is not measurement. A documented restriction can establish a mechanism without complete measurement counts. Carry uncertainty about an inferred mechanism into the participants considered for conditional impact, while allowing source-supported probable judgments.
right_facts: The same flow, contactability and unknown endpoint measurements are reported. The source additionally states that the analysis excluded all noncompleters regardless of whether their endpoint outcomes were available.

8|Our team has already reported that preoxygenation in
9|severely hypoxemic patients with HFNC compared with
10|SMO did not improve median lowest SpO2 during intu-
11|bation [3]. To our knowledge, the present study is the
12|first large multicenter randomized clinical trial assessing
13|HFNC preoxygenation before intubation in non-severely
14|hypoxemic critically ill patients. The only publication
15|available in this setting was the study by Miguel-Mon-
16|tanes et al. [15]. Their study reported an improvement in
17|the median lowest SpO2 during intubation and a reduc-
18|tion in severe oxygen desaturations when using HFNC
19|compared with face mask for preoxygenation. Although
20|it included patients with baseline characteristics close to
21|ours, the before-after and single-center design may have
22|overestimated the treatment effect, limiting the gener-
23|alization of the results and their reproducibility in mul-
24|ticenter studies. In the PROTRACH study, these trends
25|were not confirmed, but HFNC appeared as a protec-
26|tive factor for desaturation < 90% in multivariable analy-
27|sis (see Table 4). In line with previous studies [2, 6], and
28|similar to hypoxemic patients [3], our results highlighted
29|that non-severely hypoxemic patients experience numer-
30|ous life-threatening adverse events during intubation
31|including deep desaturation with minimum SpO2 of 69%
32|in HFNC vs. 43% in SMO.
33|Each complication related to preoxygenation or intu-
34|bation was immediately declared by the investigators
35|and reviewed by the safety board, ensuring high report-
36|ing accuracy. Patients undergoing HFNC preoxygenation
37|experienced fewer adverse events, including fewer severe
38|(mainly SpO2 < 80%) and moderate complications. Sev-
39|eral theoretical advantages of HFNC could explain these
40|results. HFNC has already been reported to improve
41|FRC, one of the main determinants of the duration of
42|apnea without desaturation. Reducing the risk of desatu-
43|ration, HFNC could in turn reduce complications such as
44|hypotension related to hypoxemia [24]. Compared with
45|SMO requiring two-handed thenar eminence grip to
46|perform jaw-thrust maneuver and ensure airtightness,
47|HFNC is a "hands-free" preoxygenation device that could
48|help operators to be more confident and avoid scrambled
49|intubation. Nevertheless, this aspect was not specifically
50|assessed in the study. The reduction of desaturation < 95%
51|in the HFNC group despite longer and more difficult
52|intubation could also be recognized as a marker of apneic
53|oxygenation even if this remains controversial [25]. Pre-
54|oxygenation has to be differentiated from apneic oxy-
55|genation [26]. As exhaled fraction of oxygen (EtO2) was
56|not assessed, the reduction of desaturation in HFNC
57|should not be interpreted as increased oxygen reserves
58|at the end of the preoxygenation compared with SMO.
59|However, the administration of oxygen during the apnea
60|period with HFNC could explain the lower rate of res-
61|piratory adverse events. These results are concordant
62|with the OPTINIV study [13]. This study showed that
63|in severe hypoxemic patients the preoxygenation with
64|non-invasive ventilation (NIV, namely the gold stand-
65|ard device in this setting [22, 27]) combined with HFNC
66|increased the lowest saturation during intubation com-
67|pared to NIV alone. Overall, a comprehensive improve-

24|ing daily practice in the ICUs and enhancing external
25|validity. In this setting, albeit negative in terms of the
26|primary outcome, the study provided several findings
27|suggesting that HFNC could secure intubation by reduc-
28|ing complications including desaturations. Although
29|this study enrolled ICU patients, these results could be
30|applied to all intubations in the emergency department in
31|non-severely hypoxemic patients considering that HFNC
32|is now a widespread oxygenation device.
33|This trial has several limitations. An unblinded preoxy-
34|genation device may have interfered with our findings.
35|Although feasible [13], blinding may have been very dif-
36|ficult to maintain in a large sample and multicenter trial.
37|The choice of the primary outcome can be discussed.
38|Considering the Miguel-Montanes et al. results, we
39|decided to assess minimal SpO2 instead of severe desatu-
40|ration below 80%, a common criteria which, however, is
41|infrequent in the non-severely hypoxemic patient. In the
42|same way, whether a 5% difference of SpO2 is a clinically
43|relevant endpoint may be questionable. However, such a
44|difference can lead to a decision of bag-valve mask venti-
45|lation or can initiate a fast and deep hypoxemia given the
46|sigmoidal relationship between the affinity of hemoglobin
47|for oxygen and the PaO2. In this study, the 5% difference
48|was not met. SpO2 is not the most relevant parameter
49|to assess oxygenation [28], but systematic arterial cath-
50|eterization before intubation to measure arterial oxygen
51|saturation or partial oxygen pressure could not be ethi-
52|cally defended. Similarly, EtO2 could have been a relevant
53|way to assess the quality of preoxygenation, in particular
54|to check that the preoxygenation was well performed in
55|the SMO group, with a mask correctly applied to avoid
56|leaks. It is an indicator of FRC oxygen saturation and
57|when EtO2 > 90% is achieved, preoxygenation can be
58|claimed to be effective [29]. Nevertheless, in a non-occlu-
59|sive device such as HFNC, measurement of EtO2 was dif-
60|ficult to achieve [30]. In the same way, the precise level
61|of post-apnea end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) was not
62|recorded and could have provided relevant information
63|[31]. However, we made the pragmatic choice to evalu-
64|ate SpO2, the only worldwide, non-invasive, and ready-
65|to-use device informing the attending physician on
66|apnea tolerance during intubation. Given the limitations
67|of SpO2 measurement, a research nurse was specifically
68|dedicated to monitor SpO2 throughout the procedure to
69|improve data collection. Finally, NIV was not selected as
70|the active comparator. Although it was found to improve
71|preoxygenation in obese patients in the operating room
72|[32], and in severe hypoxemic patients in ICU [22, 33],
73|no data is available in non-severely hypoxemic patients in

58|Study design, setting, and ethical considerations
59|The PROTRACH study was a multicenter, randomized,
60|controlled, open-label clinical trial. The main objective
61|was to determine the efficacy of HFNC to prevent oxy-
62|gen desaturation during intubation in the ICU compared
63|with standard of care. Patients were enrolled from April
64|2016 to June 2017 in seven French ICUs (four medical,
65|two medical-surgical, and one surgical) and followed for
66|28 days. An independent safety committee oversaw the
67|trial.

8|Randomization
9|Randomization used fixed blocks of six patients (ratio
10|1:1) and was stratified by center. The study statistician
11|generated the allocation list. Patients were allocated to
12|one of the two preoxygenation strategies using a secure
13|computer-generated online remote system controlled
14|by the independent research promotion unit at the Uni-
15|versity Hospital of Nantes which had no role in patient
16|recruitment.
17|Intervention: preoxygenation and intubation procedure
18|The study design is described in Supplement 1. Preoxy-
19|genation and intubation were performed according to
20|international recommendations in all centers [9]. The
21|intubation team was composed of one junior and one
22|senior.
23|1. Preoxygenation was started according to the rand-
24|omization group for a 4-min period [17] in a head-up
25|position. In the intervention group, preoxygenation
26|was performed with HFNC (AIRVO 2TM; Fisher &
27|Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, NZ), nasal prongs set at
28|60 L/min flow of heated and humidified pure oxygen
29|(100% fraction of inspired oxygen, 37 °C). Large or
30|medium nasal cannulae were chosen according to the
31|patient's nostril size to limit air contamination. In the
32|control group, preoxygenation was performed with
33|SMO set at 15 L/min oxygen flow with a disposable
34|self-inflating resuscitator with a reservoir bag manu-
35|ally held in place ensuring air tightness.
36|2. At the end of preoxygenation, RSI including imme-
37|diate intubation after administration of the hypnotic
38|drugs was performed in all patients. Drugs and the
39|use of a neuromuscular blocking agent were left to
40|the discretion of the physician.
41|3. During laryngoscopy and intubation, HFNC was
42|maintained in place throughout the procedure in an
43|attempt to achieve apneic oxygenation. In the control
44|group, SMO was removed in order to perform laryn-
45|goscopy.
46|4. In case of difficult intubation, the stylet was the first
47|alternative device which was proposed [18] if exter-
48|nal laryngeal manipulation did not improve glottis
49|vision.
50|5. At the end of intubation, the correct position of the
51|tracheal tube was confirmed by using capnography
52|[19].
53|Endpoints
54|The primary endpoint was the median lowest SpO2 dur-
55|ing intubation, from the beginning of the laryngoscopy
56|until the patient was connected to the mechanical ven-
57|tilator. To ensure exhaustive data collection, a research
58|nurse and an external observer concurrently collected
59|SpO2 fluctuations during the intubation.

13|Results
14|Patients
15|In the seven participating ICUs, 192 patients were rand-
16|omized in the study between April 2016 and June 2017.
17|Three patients withdrew their consent, two patients were
18|discovered to be under guardianship protection, and
19|three patients improved before the start of the study and
20|were therefore not intubated. We considered 184 patients
21|(95 in HFNC and 89 in SMO) in the intent-to-treat
22|(ITT) and 183 patients in the per-protocol (PP) analyses
23|(Fig. 1). Per-protocol analysis excluded the only patient
24|with protocol deviation in the HFNC group who did not
25|receive preoxygenation with HFNC because no device
26|was available. This patient did not present any complica-
27|tion during intubation.
